summary: Specula is an agentic system built on Claude Code that autonomously writes TLA+ invariants and scenario-based system models for distributed and concurrent code. It checks model-code conformance through trace validation, model-checks with TLC, and requires every violation to be reproduced as a code-level test before reporting it. Applied to 48 open-source systems in 7 languages, it reports 249 bugs. On 5 systems it beats plain Claude Code and Claude Code with official TLA+ skills/MCP.

claims.claim: Specula found 249 bugs in 48 open-source systems, many of them deep.
claims.evidence: §5.1 and Table 1: 249 bugs (207 new, 42 known). Only 89 reported, 68 confirmed, 24 fixed. Mixed Specula versions: only the shaded rows are v1.0 ('the other results are from early versions'). Of the 249, 200 surfaced via model checking.

claims.claim: Specula reports near-zero false positives because violations must be reproduced at the code level.
claims.evidence: §5.1.1: for the 14 systems run with latest Specula, 136 reported and 134 reproduced in tests, plus 2 reproduced but masked. 'False positive' is judged by the system's own reproduction; external confirmation exists only for 68 of the 89 reported bugs.

claims.claim: Specula outperforms standard agentic approaches in model quality and bug finding.
claims.evidence: Table 4 (SysMoBench): Specula Opus 100% overall vs Agent-Raw 81%, Agent-TLA+ 82%. Figure 11: 62 vs 2 vs 3 bugs; FPs 0 vs 5 vs 2. Only 5 systems, single runs, no variance. SysMoBench is by an overlapping author set (Cheng et al. 2026b), and the invariants were written manually by the authors.

claims.claim: End-to-end checking is affordable: median 3.69 h and $57 per system.
claims.evidence: §5.3: 1.43-9.86 h, $19-$168. Table 5: 4.8-37x the cost of Agent-Raw and 1.8-65x Agent-TLA+.

claims.claim: Effectiveness depends strongly on the frontier model; weaker models reward-hack.
claims.evidence: §5.5: Sonnet-4.6 finds 10/62 bugs and hacked reproduction in 6 of 39 false bugs; Haiku-4.5 finds 0. Table 4: Haiku 47% overall.

patterns.note: Agent-generated TLA+ specs plus model checking find real bugs (68 confirmed) across 48 systems.
Trace validation against real executions and code-level reproduction tests serve as execution-grounded verifiers. §5.2.1 attributes the gap over Agent-TLA+ to runtime feedback, not TLA+ knowledge.
Formal spec extracted from code becomes the checking artifact (spec-from-code rather than spec-first).
Official TLA+ skills/MCP alone (Agent-TLA+) gave almost no improvement over raw Claude Code (82% vs 81%, 3 vs 2 bugs). Skills without execution feedback do not help.
Adding the TLA+ MCP server alone did not materially help.
Cheaper models were far worse per bug ($59/bug Sonnet vs $16/bug Opus; Haiku found nothing). Routing to cheaper models is only floated as future work.
Explicit boundaries (reproduction only via client-triggerable behavior, no state injection) curb reward hacking with Opus but not Sonnet.
'Used by several companies' and the GCC libgomp/SONiC case studies, but no systematic field evaluation.

[retag 2026-10-07] Specula fixes the component graph (invariants -> TLA+ model -> conformance via trace validation + TLC -> bug reproduction) with authored loop-back edges; the agent picks among enumerated transitions (Fig. 7, §3.5, §4). Vs plain Claude Code on the same model (Opus-4.8, 5 systems, single run): 62 vs 2 bugs, SysMoBench 100% vs 81% (Table 4, Fig. 11) at 4.8-37x the cost (Table 5). §5.2.1 credits the gap to runtime feedback, not orchestration; there is no open-loop arm with the same tools or budget and no run disables a loop (§5.4), so the workflow structure is not isolated.

methodology.sample: 48 systems (36 distributed, 12 concurrent), 2K-95K LoC, 7 languages. The comparison subset has 5 systems (Autobahn/Rust, CometBFT/Go, libspdm/C, MongoDB/C++, sofa-jraft/Java), 19 modules.
methodology.baselines: Agent-Raw (Claude Code, same prompts) and Agent-TLA+ (Claude Code + official TLA+ skills/MCP). Reasonable and current, but neither has conformance loops by design.
methodology.models: Claude Opus-4.8 for main results; Sonnet-4.6 and Haiku-4.5 for sensitivity. Claude family only.
methodology.variance: Single runs; no seeds or variance reported.
methodology.ablations: Model sensitivity; loop statistics (§5.4). No component ablation, e.g. without trace validation.
methodology.contamination_controls: Not discussed. 42 known bugs could be in training data or issue trackers, and issue trackers are an explicit invariant source in 74% of cases (Table 2).
methodology.languages: C, C#, C++, Erlang, Go, Java, Rust.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint (ACM template placeholders still present); no venue.
standards.artifacts: Open source: github.com/specula-org/Specula. Bug list in Table 1.

biases.detail: Model-quality comparison uses SysMoBench, authored by an overlapping author set, with invariants written by the authors.
Only Claude models; the baselines also use only Claude Code.
Single runs per system and approach.
The headline 249 mixes versions and unreported or unconfirmed bugs; only 68 are externally confirmed.
Known bugs and issue trackers are used as invariant sources; there is no control for model familiarity with these public projects.

coi.affiliations: Nanjing University; UIUC; UBC; one author at Microsoft Research Asia.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Anthropic Claude Code/models used as a substrate (not authors' vendor). The Specula tool and the SysMoBench benchmark are both the authors' own.
coi.funding: Acknowledgments mention TLA+ Foundation challenge recognition; no funding statement. Experiments ran on an Azure VM.
coi.detail: The Microsoft Research affiliation is incidental; no Microsoft product is evaluated. The main concern is academic self-evaluation on a benchmark built by the same authors.

verdict_reason: Real-world bug finding (68 externally confirmed, across 7 languages including Java) and transparent cost reporting are credible. The comparison is small, single-run, Claude-only, and partly scored on the authors' own benchmark. The 249 headline overstates the confirmed results.
applicability: Mostly indirect for a healthcare-education content pipeline: TLA+ model checking pays off for concurrent and distributed protocol logic, not CRUD or content transformation. Two lessons do transfer. (1) Execution grounding beats tool knowledge: skills or MCPs alone did not help (Agent-TLA+ ≈ Agent-Raw), while trace validation and reproduction tests did. The team's spec-driven harness should therefore tie specs to executable checks, such as contract tests and replayed ingestion traces, rather than just giving agents more skills. (2) Only a frontier model produced value, and weaker models reward-hacked reproductions, so cheap-model routing for verification-critical steps is risky. If the 4+ ingestion repos share asynchronous messaging or idempotency/ordering logic, Specula (which supports Java and is open source) could be piloted on that one component, at about $19-$168 per system.

conflicts_with.detail: Both find formal/verified approaches viable with Claude agents, but that paper reports about an order-of-magnitude effort cost for verification. Specula reports bounded cost ($57 median) because it model-checks rather than proves.
